# What problems will I have if I use a rusted input shaft on a transmission?

Installing a 25-year-old BMW E36 transmission that has sat outdoors introduces specific mechanical risks beyond simple surface rust. The white scale you observed in the bell housing and along the input shaft indicates prolonged exposure to moisture, likely leading to galvanic corrosion or general oxidation of the steel components. While cleaning with wet-and-dry sandpaper (600â1200 grit) and WD-40 restored manual sliding capability, this is a superficial fix that does not address the underlying metallurgical changes caused by pitting.

The most immediate concern is the interaction between the input shaft and the pilot bearing on the engine. The input shaft slides into the pilot bearing (or bushing) located in the crankshaft nose. This interface relies on precise tolerances to maintain concentricity while allowing axial movement for clutch engagement. If the shaft surface exhibits pitting, even after aggressive cleaning, you risk creating a high point or an uneven mating surface.

When the transmission is installed, the input shaft must slide smoothly into the engine bay. However, once the clutch assembly is locked onto the flywheel and the torque converter (if applicable) or engine block is secured, the input shaft is under load. A pitted shaft can lead to premature wear of the pilot bearing because the bearing rollers will roll over the irregularities in the shaft. Over time, this uneven stress can cause the pilot bearing to seize or develop excessive play, resulting in vibration that travels up through the drivetrain to the engine mounts and chassis.

Furthermore, there is a critical risk regarding oil contamination. The input shaft seal sits at the junction between the transmission and the engine crankshaft. If you decide to replace this seal, it is vital to ensure the mating surface on the transmission case and the shaft end are perfectly clean. Rust particles that remain in the spline grooves or pitting deep enough to catch debris can act as abrasives inside the gear train. As the clutch packs shift, these abrasive particles can be ground into the friction material of the clutch discs or the release bearing race. This accelerates wear and can lead to total clutch failure much sooner than expected.

Your hesitation about replacing the input shaft is understandable given the cost of a rebuilt transmission unit. However, you must weigh the cost of a new shaft against the potential cost of a seized pilot bearing or ruined clutch assembly. In many cases, the input shaft is relatively inexpensive compared to the labor required to remove and reinstall the entire transmission again to replace failed components.

If you proceed with installation, ensure that any residual moisture from cleaning is completely evaporated before applying fresh grease. Use a high-quality synthetic grease on the splines, but avoid over-greasing, as excess grease can be forced into areas where it isn't needed or attract more contaminants. Monitor the transmission closely for unusual noises upon initial startup, specifically grinding sounds that indicate shaft binding or bearing noise.

Ultimately, while the input shaft may function mechanically after cleaning, the pitting represents a deviation from original specifications. If the vehicle is intended for long-term reliability, sourcing a replacement input shaft or having one machined to remove deep pits (if structurally sound) is often the safer engineering decision than running a compromised component in an expensive drivetrain system.
